title: Real incidents of agents causing damage + state of automated failure attribution
outcome: A sourced incident catalogue and attribution evidence that make the problem concrete for the framing and give us realistic test scenarios
acceptance: ≥6 real incidents with primary/first-hand URLs (e.g. Replit DB deletion Jul 2025, AI Incident Database entries), each with: what broke, who detected, time-to-detect/contain/recover if known, how recovered
Summary of Who&When (arXiv 2505.00212) and ≥1 follow-up: exact reported attribution accuracies with dataset/setting
Pattern analysis: which incidents a per-agent selective rollback would have fixed vs. not
'Implications for framing' and 'Implications for our design' sections (incl. 3 candidate demo scenarios)
summary:
Report at research/RES-07.md: 7 incidents catalogued (Replit, Gemini CLI, Claude Code x2, Antigravity, AWS/Kiro (disputed), PocketOS) with AIID/GitHub/company sources; none is multi-agent, and attribution was trivial in all (one agent). Pain was irreversibility, backups inside blast radius, agent self-misreporting, human detection after the fact; durations rarely public.
Who&When verified: abstract headline best 53.5% agent / 14.2% step (cell not found in body tables); GPT-4o Table 1 ranges 26-55% agent, 3.5-25.5% step vs random 12-29 / 4-19. Follow-ups FAMAS (57.61/29.35 overall), CHIEF (77.59/29.31 hand; 76.80/52.00 alg-gen), DoVer, MAST.
Pattern: selective rollback alone fixes few of the incidents; pre-execution gating, scoped identity and out-of-reach pre-images matter more. 3 demo scenarios included.
Top framing implication: lead with 'seconds to break, days to repair, and nobody can say who/what from logs' but do not claim multi-agent incidents exist; use LLM attribution as the baseline provenance beats.
